A composite input is one quote series of one provider that a composite reads. The inputs of a composite are
read in the order of their position. The set of inputs also says which providers a party needs the derived right
on, and which items the service demands on a party's behalf when the party uses the composite.

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
A composite is an internal item that the service derives from several quote series by a rule. A blended
EUR/USD spot from Bloomberg and LSEG is the first case. The composite is published by an internal provider with
one source of kind derived. It has no rate card: its use counts as demand on its inputs.
A party that uses a composite needs the derived right on the provider of every input. A composite with a
missing right gets no values and shows the reason. The rule is named by a code, so a later rule needs no schema
change. The system tenant owns the rows and every tenant reads them.

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
The detail row of one marketdata.curve_publish approval request: the subject
the request authorises, and the record of the act once the subject is published.
A request is a header. What it is about lives here, keyed by the request's own
id, exactly as a proposed book change lives in ores.refdata.book_change and is
keyed by its request. The subject is three facts and no more: the curve
configuration whose output is published, the as-of instant the bootstrap reads
the market at, and the party the configuration belongs to (party_id). The curve
is named by its configuration because that is what the publish call names. The
series the output is written to (output_series_id) is carried beside it because
the reader that serves a published curve starts from a series and not from a
published_at and published_by are the publication record. Both are empty
while the request waits, and both are written in one act when the approved
subject is published: the timestamp is the instant the published set moved, and
the username is the account that applied it. The row is bitemporal, so the
applied version is a new version of the same row and the history holds the
unapplied subject beside it. request_id is the natural key, so a request
authorises one publish and no second apply can find a row to write.
A set ends once, and the end is two more facts on the same row rather than a
second entity. withdrawn_at, withdrawn_by, withdrawn_reason_code and
withdrawal_request_id are the withdrawal: the instant, the account, the reason
and the request that authorised it, written as a new version of this row. The
withdrawal is not a deletion: the published facts stay, so the set a desk priced
from is still readable afterwards. superseded_at,
superseded_by_request_id and superseded_as_of are the supersession: a later
publish replaced this set, and the link names the successor's request and the
as-of it was built at. A supersession is a publish and not a second act, so the
successor's own apply writes it on this row.
The state a reader sees is a function of these facts and is stored nowhere:
withdrawn when withdrawn_at holds an instant, superseded when superseded_at
does, published when published_at does, and a candidate otherwise.
The row is not a client's to write: the raise writes it, the gate reads it, and
the apply stamps it. A client reads it to decide a request or to audit a curve.

A delivery count is a fact about usage. The fan-out counts the ticks it delivers to each party for each item
and writes the counts in batches. A count holds no price. The only cost at tick time is one increment in
memory, and one row is written for each party, item and hour at each write.
A row counts the deliveries since the last write, so the rating step adds the rows of an hour.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
A demand interval is a fact about usage. It records that one item was in the demand set of a party, and
so was published by the source that served the party, from one time to another. Demand is a control
signal for the adapter and a billing fact for the vendor: a live adapter pays for the items in the set.
The service opens an interval when an item enters the demand of a party and closes it when the item
leaves, or when the party stops being served by the source.

A mapping links a vendor instrument (provider, id scheme, external id, field) to an
internal item, which is an oresmd datum. It belongs to the provider and not to a
source, so the live and the simulated sources of one provider share it and a party
that changes its source keeps its series. The mapping is many to one: several vendor
instruments, of different providers, can map to one item.
A mapping holds for a period. A vendor instrument has at most one mapping that starts
at a given instant. The system tenant and the system party own the rows. Every
tenant reads them and only the system tenant writes them.

A source is one adapter instance of a provider: bloomberg-a and
bloomberg-b are two sources of the provider bloomberg. Its kind says how the
adapter gets its values and is data a person can read. No code in the pipeline
branches on it. The name is a label and no code parses it.
A provider can have several sources at once. A party reaches one of them through a
route, never through the provider. One source of each provider is the default, and a
The system tenant and the system party own the rows. Every tenant reads them and
only the system tenant writes them.

system needs, the system mints an id in the vendor's style, sets minted and writes
A mapping links a vendor instrument to an internal item. The system tenant and the

A historical index fixing: the official value of a fixing index (identified via
series_id) on a given fixing_date. Separate from observations: fixings are
historical facts (e.g. EUR-EURIBOR-3M fixed at X on date Y) rather than
TimescaleDB hypertable partitioned by fixing_date with 30-day chunks.
Corrections use the soft-update/soft-delete pattern (no GIST, no DELETE RULEs).
No audit trail columns — volume makes them impractical.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
A single market data observation: the value of a series at a given
observation_datetime is the financial valid-time (UTC); valid_from/valid_to
is the transaction time. Corrections replace the previous value via the
TimescaleDB hypertable partitioned by observation_datetime with 30-day chunks;
GIST exclusion and DELETE RULEs are incompatible with hypertables — uniqueness
is enforced via partial unique index and the soft-update/soft-delete trigger pair.
No audit trail columns (version, modified_by, performed_by, change_reason_code,
change_commentary) — tick-level data volumes make these impractical.

A market series is a container of observations, and the asset classes it
serves follow from what it observes rather than from a single value on
the series itself. Most series belong to exactly one class, but a
pairwise correlation relates two -- an equity index against an FX rate,
say -- and belongs to both. A not-null column cannot hold that, so the

A projection of market_series.oresmd_uri, one row per series, so a query can
join on the series and filter on a real column. The URI stays the only spelling
the system writes and the codec stays the only thing that reads it; this table is
written from that parse, never read back to rebuild a URI.
The column set is the identity fields the codec admits, one column per field
the instrument schema marks field_role::identity, and one column per field the
index grammar declares, because a fixing's whole ORE index name is its identity,
plus the columns that say which kind of identity the row carries. A field the
type's schema row, or the family's index row, does not declare is empty, because
the row holds only the columns its own grammar fills. A column is text, not a
typed relational form, because the codec keeps every value as the key spelled it
and a projection that reinterpreted it would be a second spelling of the same
The table is a current state, not a history: the series row is already temporal
and the identity does not change under it, so one row per series is enough and
the primary key is the series. The column list is checked against the codec
schema by build/scripts/check_marketdata_identity_columns.py, so the two cannot
The identity the decomposed columns spell is unique per party, as the series URI
is. A fixing row states that at the table: a unique index over its context and
its index-grammar columns, with nulls not distinct so an empty field counts as
equal to an empty field, refuses two fixings that spell one identity. A series
row cannot carry such an index, because its identity spans the whole instrument
schema, more columns than an index may hold; the series table's own unique URI
and the decomposition's injectivity are what keep it single.

A catalog entry for a market data series — it records what is being observed:
a yield curve, vol surface, spot rate, fixing index, or similar. Standard
temporal reference data; changes infrequently so a regular table with GIST
The series is identified by oresmd_uri, the series URI of the datum its ORE
key names, or the fixing URI of its index name. The URI holds every field of the
series' identity, so the table keeps no decomposed copy of the key;
series_subclass carries the coarse taxonomy for filtering, and the asset
classes the series belongs to live in
market_series_asset_classes -- a set rather than a column, because a
pairwise correlation relates two classes at once.
whether this series is directly observed (the sentinel OBSERVED) or
derived by a named mechanism (e.g. IR_CURVE_BOOTSTRAP,
CRM_DERIVATION) -- so any published series answers "was this observed
or computed, and by what" without guessing from the source tag on its
observations. Per-observation lineage (which source series/as-of a
specific derived point came from) is a separate concern, tracked by
provider_code names the provider whose ids the series carries. A series is one
item of one provider held by one party, so two providers that quote the same item
keep two series, and a party that switches the source of a provider keeps one
series and one history. The observations beneath it record the source that
produced each one, for information; the source is never part of the key.

Per-observation provenance for a bare market_observation row whose source
is not the market's own quote: which derivation config/version produced it,
and which upstream source series/as-of it read, or -- for a point an operator
keyed by hand -- which kind of point it is, who keyed it and why. Written
never for the common quoted case, and never as a column on
documented as carrying no audit columns because tick-level volumes make
point_source_kind names the two kinds that carry an annex row: derived
for a point a derivation created, and manual for one keyed by hand.
*Quoted is the absence of a row*, so a quoted tick keeps writing one row to
the hot hypertable and nothing else; the invariant this rests on is that a
point a derivation created always has an annex row.
Deliberately generic, not curve-specific: this is what lets CRM's own
derived-cross publishing (currently pull-only -- see the CRM
architecture decision to never broadcast the full derived set as
ticks) reuse this table unchanged whenever it starts persisting,
stamping derivation_kind to 'CRM_DERIVATION' exactly as the IR
triggers), not a hypertable: unlike market_observations, lineage rows
are written only for the minority of observations that are derived, so
tick-level volume concerns that justify market_observations's own
hypertable/no-audit-columns treatment do not apply here. A rerun of a
derivation over the same tenor/point natural key closes the prior
generation's lineage row and inserts a new one -- the same soft-update
convention every other bitemporal entity in this codebase already
gets, mirroring (not literally reusing) how market_observations

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
The catalogue of market data providers: data vendors such as Bloomberg and LSEG,
exchanges such as CME, brokers, and reference sets such as the ORE examples. A
provider owns a namespace of vendor ids. Every source belongs to one provider, and
every vendor instrument and mapping belongs to a provider, so a live and a
simulated source of one provider share their ids and their mapping. The name
carries no mark of any source kind.
The system tenant and the system party own the rows. Every tenant reads them and
only the system tenant writes them.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
A rate card belongs to a source. It is the set of components that apply to the source in a period. Each
component has a driver, which says what the vendor counts, and a charge for one unit of it. A rating step
applies the components to the usage events of a period and gives the bill of the source.
A simulated source carries a card of its own with illustrative charges, or published ones where they
exist. The model is the same for every source, so a simulated source gives a shadow bill with the same
lines as a live one. The system tenant owns the cards, because the platform owns the vendor contracts.

A route names the one source that serves a party for a provider. A party has at most one
route for each provider, so it reads one value of each instrument and the mapping and the series
key stay unambiguous. A source switch is one new route and nothing else.
The source must belong to the provider of the route, and the party must hold a subscription to
the provider. A change of route is a new version with a reason and a commentary, and the history
keeps the earlier routes. The source must also be ready; the adapter state that says so is held by

The axes a composite market series varies over. A term structure varies over one
axis and a surface over two. Each row names one field the series' instrument type
marks as a coordinate, so the object's shape is a declared thing rather than an
inference from whatever points happen to be stored.
The rows are ordered. The sequence column holds the position of each axis among
the object's coordinates, so a reader walks the axes in the order the type's key
writes them and a hole in a grid is a hole rather than an absent row.
The table is a current state, not a history: the series row is already temporal
and the shape of a series is written again whenever it is built. A series with no
rows here declares no shape, and a caller that reads one gets nothing rather than

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
One value an axis of a composite market series holds. The rows of one axis are
its ordered values, so a grid can be read as coordinates rather than as the set
of points that survived a build.
The sequence column holds the position of each value among its axis's values.
A value that the axis declares and no point uses is still a declared value, and
a reader can tell it apart from a value the build never saw.
The table is a current state, not a history: a rebuilt series writes its shape
again. A value is text because the codec keeps every value as the key spelled
it, and a projection that reinterpreted it would be a second spelling of the

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
The taxonomy rule for a market series, one row per identity the runtime
classifies. The runtime reads the whole table once, builds a classifier from it,
and asks that classifier for the asset classes and the series subclass of every
The table replaces a compiled C++ map, so the taxonomy is managed like every
other catalogue: an instrument a corpus adds later, or one a user brings, is an
inserted row rather than a rebuild. This matters because an ingest that cannot
classify a series it must create aborts on it, so a compiled table makes every
The key is the oresmd identity and not an ORE key. Two kinds of identity reach
this table, and key_kind says which a row is keyed by:
- datum, keyed by instrument -- the text the URI writes under
instrument, such as ir_swap or discount -- and by quote, the text it
writes under quote, or the empty string for a rule that applies to every
quote of its instrument. Most instruments classify the same way whatever their
quote carries, so their row holds the empty string; a lookup tries the exact
quote first and falls back to the empty one.
- index, keyed by instrument too, which for this kind holds the index
family's oresmd name or the empty string for every family. A fixing series is
an index and not a datum, so it is keyed by the index's own vocabulary.
asset_class_source says where a row's classes come from:
- literal names its class in asset_class_code.
- correlation_operands reads the classes from the two operand fields of a
correlation datum, because a pairwise correlation belongs to the two classes
it relates and to no class of its own.
- index_authority reads the class from the index family's schema row, whose
asset authority names the market-data namespace the index is written in, and
ores.refdata.asset_class_catalogue maps that authority onto a refdata class.
One row serves every index family, and a family the catalogue maps to no class
leaves the class list empty rather than mis-classing the series.
The class codes name rows in refdata.asset_class_code and the subclass codes
name rows in refdata.series_subclass_code, and the insert trigger checks both
The reader rejects an empty table, because an empty table aborts the first
ingest that reads it and the message should name the table rather than the first

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
A subscription interval is a fact about usage. It records that a party held a subscription to a provider
with given rights and was routed to a source, from one time to another. It holds no price. A rating
step applies the rate card of the source to the interval later, so a new contract can price old facts.
The service opens an interval when a route and its subscription come to hold together and closes it
when either changes or ends. A change of the source or of the rights closes one interval and opens the
next. A party administrator reads the intervals of the party and the system tenant reads all of them.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
A subscription is the entitlement of one party to the feeds of one provider. It carries the
three rights the vendor licences name: display, non_display and derived. A demand checks
that the subscription holds the right the use needs. The source that serves the party is not
A subscription holds at least one right. A party administrator reads and changes only the
subscriptions of the party, and the history of every change is kept.
A tick row stores its datum as a small number, not as the URI text. This table says which
datum each number means within one series. A series without coordinates has one datum, and
so one row. The numbers of a series start at 1 and stay for as long as the series exists,
because a tick row refers to them. The URI is the one the feed sent, which is the URI of the
The ingest assigns a number the first time it sees a datum, so the table is small and cold:
one row for each distinct datum of a series. The ingest context names no party, so the
table has the tenant policy only, as the observation table has, and a reader states the

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
A tick is a value of a series at a time, and the series has one owner, a tenant and a
party, so each row carries the owner of its series. The ingest copies the owner from the
The table has no trigger, no valid_to and one index on the series and the time. A
correction is a new row, and the reader takes the latest. There is no notification trigger:
the live path publishes the tick, and the table is the history.
Row-level security uses the policies of the other tables, in the scalar subquery form. The
session functions that the other tables call cost about 8 to 10 microseconds for each
filtered row, because the planner calls them again for every row, and a subquery around the
setting makes it evaluate the setting once for each query. FORCE makes the policies apply
The marketdata tick writer role has BYPASSRLS and INSERT only. PostgreSQL refuses COPY into
a table with row-level security for a role that the policies apply to, and this role is
exempt. It does not own the table and has no SELECT.
The table is not compressed, because row-level security is not supported on compressed
chunks. Retention drops whole chunks. See doc/knowledge/architecture/tick_ingest_pipeline.org.
